t.2.16.1: Rāma saw his father seated on a splendid seat together with Kaikeyī, wretched, with a face that was withering away.
t.2.16.2: He first saluted his father's feet in a humble manner, and then, with a fully composed mind, he paid homage at the feet of Kaikeyī.
t.2.16.3: Having uttered only the word “Rāma!”, the wretched king, his eyes brimming with tears, could neither look at him nor speak to him.
t.2.16.4: Seeing that unprecedented, fear-inspiring appearance of the lord of men, Rāma too was seized with fear, as if he had touched a serpent with his foot.
t.2.16.5: Him, the great king, his senses cheerless, worn down by grief and anguish, sighing, his mind pained and bewildered.
t.2.16.6: He was like the wave-garlanded ocean, imperturbable by nature, now churning in agitation, like the sun overwhelmed by eclipse, like a seer who has spoken an untruth.
t.2.16.7: For, perceiving that grief of his father, which was all but unthinkable, he grew more agitated still, like the ocean at the full moon.
t.2.16.8: And then Rāma, devoted to his father's welfare, reflected: "Why is it that the king does not welcome me today?"
t.2.16.9: At other times, even when angry, my father grows gracious on seeing me. Why, then, does distress arise in him today as he looks upon me?
t.2.16.10: Afflicted with grief and looking almost wretched, the radiance of his face dimmed with dejection, Rāma first saluted Kaikeyī and then spoke these words.
t.2.16.11: Surely I have not, out of ignorance, committed some offense by which my father has become angry? Tell me that, and you yourself must appease him.
t.2.16.12: Pale-faced and dejected, he does not speak to me. Is some bodily or mental pain or torment not afflicting him? For happiness is always hard to attain.
t.2.16.13: I hope nothing inauspicious has befallen Prince Bharata, so pleasing to behold, or the great-spirited Śatrughna, or my mothers?
t.2.16.14: Failing to please the great king, or not carrying out my father's word, I would not wish to live even for a moment while the king is angry.
t.2.16.15: How could a man not abide by the will of the one in whom he sees the very root of his own coming into being in this world, when that deity stands visibly before him?
t.2.16.16: Can it be that you, out of pride and in anger, spoke some harsh word to my father, and that this is why his mind is so troubled?
t.2.16.17: Tell me this truly, O queen, as I ask you: for what reason has this unprecedented change come over the lord of men?
t.2.16.18: For at the word of the king I would even fall into fire, swallow deadly poison, or sink into the ocean, when commanded by him who is my guru, my father, my king, and my well-wisher.
t.2.16.19: Therefore tell me, O queen, the word that the king desires; I will do it, and I give my promise: Rāma does not speak twice.
t.2.16.20: To that Rāma, endowed with uprightness and speaking the truth, the ignoble Kaikeyī spoke words exceedingly harsh.
t.2.16.21: Long ago, O Rāghava, in the war between the gods and the asuras, your father, pierced by an arrow in that great battle and protected by me, granted me two boons.
t.2.16.22: Thereupon the king was asked by me for the consecration of Bharata and for your going to the Daṇḍaka forest this very day, O Rāghava.
t.2.16.24: So abide by your father's command, just as he has promised: you must enter the forest for nine years and five.
t.2.16.23: If you wish to make your father true to his promise, and yourself as well, O best of men, then listen to these words of mine.
t.2.16.25: Giving up this consecration, live for seven and seven years in the Daṇḍaka forest, having taken refuge there, wearing matted locks and garments of bark.
t.2.16.26: Let Bharata, from the city of Kosala, rule this earth, strewn with many kinds of jewels and filled with horses, chariots and elephants.
t.2.16.27: Having heard that unpleasant speech, which was like death, Rāma, the slayer of foes, was not distressed, and he said this to Kaikeyī.
t.2.16.28: So be it! I shall go from here to dwell in the forest, wearing matted locks and garments of bark, faithfully keeping the king's promise.
t.2.16.29: But this I wish to know: for what reason does the lord of the earth, the invincible subduer of foes, not greet me with joy as before?
t.2.16.30: You must not be angry, O queen; speak, and before your very eyes I shall go to the forest, wearing bark garments and matted locks. Be well pleased.
t.2.16.31: When commanded in confidence by the king, my well-wisher, my elder and my father, who is mindful of service done, what pleasing thing would I not do?
t.2.16.33: For I myself would gladly give Sītā, the kingdom, my cherished life, and my wealth to my brother Bharata, even unasked.
t.2.16.32: But one pain in my mind seems to burn my heart: that the king did not himself tell me of Bharata's consecration.
t.2.16.34: How much more, then, when I am urged by my father himself, the lord of men, and am keeping his promise for the sake of fulfilling your cherished wish?
t.2.16.35: Therefore do you console him; what is this, that the lord of the earth, his eyes fixed upon the ground, slowly sheds tears?
t.2.16.36: And let messengers go this very day, by the king's command, on horses of swift speed, to bring Bharata back from the house of his maternal uncle.
t.2.16.37: Here I am, going from here in haste to the Daṇḍaka forest, without questioning my father's word, to dwell there for fourteen years.
t.2.16.38: Delighted on hearing those words of Rāma, Kaikeyī, trusting that he would indeed depart, urged Rāghava to make haste.
t.2.16.39: So be it. Messengers, men mounted on swift-paced horses, will go to bring Bharata back from the house of his maternal uncle.
t.2.16.40: But I do not think delay is fitting for you, eager as you are; therefore, Rāma, you ought to go quickly from here to the forest.
t.2.16.41: And that the king, overcome with shame, does not himself speak to you, this is nothing at all, O best of men; let this resentment be put away.
t.2.16.42: Until you have hastened from this city and gone to the forest, O Rāma, your father will neither bathe nor even eat.
t.2.16.43: Crying "Alas, how dreadful!" and sighing deeply, the king, flooded with grief, fell senseless upon that gold-adorned couch.
t.2.16.44: Rāma, too, having raised the king, and spurred on by Kaikeyī like a horse struck with a whip, made haste to go to the forest.
t.2.16.45: Having heard that unpleasant speech of the ignoble woman, cruel at its core, Rāma, free from distress, spoke these words to Kaikeyī.
t.2.16.46: I am not one bent on wealth, O queen, nor do I wish to dwell in the world for its sake; know me to be like the seers, devoted to dharma alone.
t.2.16.47: Whatever pleasing thing can be done by me for your honour, even at the cost of giving up my life, consider it in every way already done.
t.2.16.48: For there is no practice of dharma greater than this: obedient service to one's father, or the carrying out of his word.
t.2.16.49: Even though His Majesty has not told me himself, at your word, my lady, I shall dwell here in the lonely forest for fourteen years.
t.2.16.50: Surely, Kaikeyī, you credit me with no virtue at all, since you spoke to the king when you yourself have even greater authority over me.
t.2.16.51: As soon as I take leave of my mother and win Sītā over, I shall go this very day to the great forest of the Daṇḍakas.
t.2.16.52: You must act in such a way that Bharata may rule the kingdom and obey his father, for that is the eternal dharma.
t.2.16.53: Hearing Rāma's words, his father, deeply stricken with sorrow, was unable through grief to hold back his tears and wept with a loud cry.
t.2.16.54: Then the greatly radiant Rāma, having saluted the feet of his senseless father and also of the ignoble Kaikeyī, went forth.
t.2.16.55: Rāma, having circumambulated his father and Kaikeyī, went out from that inner apartment and saw his own friends.
t.2.16.56: Lakṣmaṇa, who increased the joy of Sumitrā, followed behind him, his eyes brimming with tears and himself filled with intense anger.
t.2.16.58: The loss of the kingdom does not diminish his great splendor, the beloved of the world, just as night does not diminish the loveliness of the cool-rayed moon.
t.2.16.57: Having reverently circumambulated the vessels prepared for the consecration, Rāma slowly departed, full of regard, without letting his gaze waver there.
t.2.16.59: No disturbance of mind was seen in him, though he wished to go to the forest and was giving up the earth, as in one who has passed beyond all worlds.
t.2.16.60: Bearing his sorrow within his mind and restraining his senses, the self-possessed one, bearer of unwelcome tidings, entered his mother's dwelling.
t.2.16.61: Entering the dwelling that was exceedingly full of joy, and perceiving that this ruin of his fortunes had come upon him, Rāma showed no change of feeling there, fearing that his loved ones might themselves be undone by it.
